Imagine you're going on a road trip. You plan ahead and pay for the big things — your hotel room and your gas. Those are your main expenses. But along the way, you also end up spending a little money on things you didn't specifically plan for: a bottle of water at a gas station, a tip for the hotel staff, a pay-per-use parking meter, an aspirin from a vending machine. None of these were the point of your trip. They just... happened on the side.

Those small, minor, secondary costs are incidentals.

In its most common noun form, incidentals (almost always used in the plural) refers to minor expenses that are secondary to the main cost of something — small charges that come up alongside a bigger, more important purchase or activity.

The heart of the word is this idea: something "incidental" is not the main event. It is a side thing — something that happens in connection with something bigger, but is not the focus itself.

So when that side thing costs you money, it becomes an incidental expense — or simply, an incidental. Collect a bunch of them together and you have incidentals.

Think of it this way:

  • The hotel room = the main expense.
  • The phone call you made from the hotel room, the minibar snack, the room service tip = incidentals.
  • The airline ticket = the main expense.
  • The luggage cart fee, the airport lounge coffee, the travel-size shampoo you had to buy = incidentals.
  • Your monthly salary = your main income.
  • The small reimbursements, petty cash expenses, or miscellaneous work costs = incidentals.

To truly understand this word, notice that incidentals tend to share a few qualities:

1. They are minor in size. Incidentals are never the big-ticket items. They are the small stuff — individually, they seem almost trivial. It's only when you add them all up that they can sometimes surprise you.

2. They are secondary in importance. They exist because of something else. You wouldn't have these costs at all if not for the main activity happening alongside them. You only need that hotel-room phone charge because you're already staying at the hotel.

3. They are often unpredictable or unspecified in advance. When someone budgets for a business trip, they can plan for the flight and the hotel with precision. But incidentals are the fuzzy, hard-to-predict extras that vary from person to person and trip to trip. You might not know exactly what they'll be until they happen.

4. They are miscellaneous by nature. Incidentals don't fit neatly into one specific category. They are a catch-all for the various small things that don't deserve their own line in a budget.
Where You'll Commonly See This Word

In travel and hotels: This is the most frequent place you'll encounter the word. When you check into a hotel, the staff will often ask for a credit card to cover "incidentals." This means they are taking a temporary hold on a small amount of money to cover any minor charges you might create during your stay — like using the minibar, ordering room service, making phone calls, or using the gym towel service. Once you check out and nothing is owed, the hold is released. The hotel isn't accusing you of anything; it's simply protecting itself against the unpredictable small costs you might generate.

In business and work expenses: When an employee travels for work, a company might reimburse them for their flights, hotel, and meals — but also for "incidentals," meaning the small, miscellaneous costs that don't fit into a named category: a tip here, a printing charge there, a taxi to an unexpected meeting.

In budgeting and finance: When people plan budgets — whether for a project, a wedding, a vacation, or a business — they often set aside a separate fund simply called "incidentals" or an "incidentals budget." This is a deliberate catch-all pool of money meant to absorb the minor, unexpected costs that are guaranteed to pop up but impossible to itemize in advance.

In everyday conversation: You might hear someone say, "The conference itself is free, but factor in incidentals like parking, lunch, and printing." They mean: the small surrounding costs that come with the main activity.

Incidentals are not the same as unexpected emergencies. If your car breaks down on that road trip, the repair cost is a surprise — but it's too large and too serious to be called an "incidental." The word carries a sense of smallness and relative unimportance. Incidentals are the minor side costs of life, not the dramatic curveballs.

Also, incidentals aren't necessarily bad or unwanted. They are simply a natural, almost inevitable part of doing anything substantial. Any experienced traveler, event planner, or businessperson knows: wherever there's a main activity, incidentals will follow. Wise people budget for them rather than being caught off guard.

Though the plural "incidentals" is by far the more common noun form, you can occasionally encounter the singular "an incidental" to refer to just one such minor item. For example: "The tip for the bellboy was just an incidental." But in practice, these small items come in groups, which is why the plural is almost always used.

Incidentals are the small, minor, secondary expenses that naturally arise alongside a main activity or purchase — too small and miscellaneous to plan for individually, but real enough that wise people budget for them as a group.
